[[File:Crypt at St Paul's Valletta.jpg|thumb|Burial place of Saviour Montebello (1762–1809) beneath the parish church of St Paul Shipwreck in Valletta]]

'''Saviour Montebello''' (9 June 1762 – 18 April 1809) was a Maltese [[Doctor of Theology]], a professor of [[philosophy]] at the [[University of Malta]], and a [[Parish priest]] of [[Bormla]].<ref>Mifsud Bonnici (1960), 368; Abela (1999); Montebello (2001), vol. II, 102.</ref> After [[Napoleon]] took over the [[Maltese islands]] in 1798, Montebello took an active part in the [[Siege of Malta (1798–1800)|resistance of the Maltese against the French]] around his home-town at [[Żejtun]]. Afterwards, when the French Napoleonic forces had been ousted, and the British set up a provisional government in [[Malta]], he was the first to be appointed to the Chair of Philosophy at the University of Malta. He held the office for almost four years, mainly teaching [[logic]] and [[metaphysics]]. He relinquished the Chair because he was appointed parish priest of [[Bormla]], the last to hold the office under this title because subsequently the parish was promoted to a [[Collegiate church|Collegiate]] led by [[Archpriests]]. He held the office of parish priest for only five years due to his premature death at age 46.<ref>No portrait or contemporary image of Montebello seems to exist.</ref>

==Biography==

===Birth and formation===

Saviour Montebello,<ref>Contemporary records give the surname in various forms: ''Montebello'', ''Montibello'' or ''Mongibello'', interchanging from one to the other indiscriminately. The latter two correspond to the dialect pronunciation of the former, and not (as Cassar 2003, under 'Montebello') claims, that they are three different surnames altogether.</ref> son of Joseph (1730<ref>APZ, ''Registrum Baptizatorum'' [''Reg. Bapt.''], MS 515, fol. 11<sup>v</sup>. Joseph was born on 3 April. His parents were Victor and Theresa Montebello.</ref>–1768<ref>''Ibid.'', ''Registrum Defunctorum'' [''Reg. Defun.''], MS 565, fol. 150. He died on 22 April at 38 years of age.</ref>) and Catherine ([[née]]; 1731<ref>''Ibid.'', ''Reg. Bapt.'', MS 515, fol. 17<sup>r</sup>. Catherine was born on 9 April. Her parents were Joseph and Mary Caruana.</ref>–?<ref>Attempts to locate her death records have unfortunately proved futile.</ref>), was born at [[Żejtun]], [[Malta]], on 9 June 1762.<ref>''Ibid.'', ''Reg. Bapt.'', MS 518, fol. 128<sup>v</sup>.</ref> His parents had married at Żejtun parish church of [[St. Catherine of Alexandria]] on 26 September 1752.<ref>''Ibid.'', ''Registrum Matrimonium'' [''Reg. Matrim.''], MS 573, fol. 5.</ref> and Saviour was their fourth child out of six.<ref>His siblings were Grace (born on 27 December 1754), Mary (5 September 1756), Michelangelo (17 December 1758), Vincentia (9 December 1764) and Elizabeth (8 July 1767). See, respectively: ''Ibid.'', ''Reg. Bapt.'', MS 518, fols. 71<sup>r</sup>, 89<sup>r</sup> and 105<sup>v</sup>, and MS 516, fols. 5 and 42.</ref> He was baptised on the same day of his birth at Żejtun's parish church by the deputy [[parish priest]], Joseph Saliba, and given the names Saviour, Francis Xavier and Anthony. His godparents were Joseph Buttigieg, son of Luke, and Rose, wife of Francis Bugeja, both from the Żejtun parish.<ref>''Ibid.'', fol. 128<sup>v</sup>.</ref>

At the age of 19, in 1781, Montebello entered the bishop's seminary at [[Floriana]] to study for the priesthood.<ref>''Ibid.''</ref> As was required at the time, his family donated him with a patrimony which could pay for his seminary expenses. This consisted of four properties: two partitions of grasslands around ''[[Tas-Silġ]]'' (limits of Żejtun), and two edifices at Żejtun's village centre. The patrimony was temporarily entrusted to the administration of Michael Pulis,<ref>''Ibid.''</ref> the husband of Montebello's older sister, Mary.<ref>They had married on 11 January 1778. See APZ, ''Reg. Matrim.'', MS 574, fol. 104.</ref>

Montebello was ordained a priest in 1787, six years after entering the seminary,<ref>Abela (1999), 49.</ref> most probably by the then [[Bishop (Catholic Church)|Bishop]] of [[Malta]], [[Carmelo Scicluna]] (bishop between 1875 and 1888).<ref>{{Catholic-hierarchy|bishop|bscic|Archbishop Carmelo Scicluna|21 January 2015}}</ref> Thereafter, Montebello seems to have been stably assigned to pastoral work within and around the parish of [[Żejtun]]. Such work does not appear to have hindered him from studying for his [[Doctorate]] in [[Theology]]. This seems to have been done in [[Malta]] (and not abroad). In this case his studies would probably have been pursued, as was normally done, at the ''[[Collegium Melitense]]'' in [[Valletta]]. By 1797, that is ten years after his [[ordination]], he had already acquired his [[S.T.D.]]<ref>Abela (1999), 49.</ref>

===Family relations===

Montebello was well connected through his family. His cousin, Giuseppe Montebello (1713<ref>APT, ''Reg. Bapt.'', vol. 3, fol. 108. He was born on 11 June.</ref>–1833<ref>''Ibid.'', ''Reg. Defun.'', vol. 5, fol. 107<sup>r</sup>. He died on 18 February, not on the 8th, as many contend, including http://www.tarxienlocalcouncil.org/?module=content&id=490</ref>), from [[Tarxien]], was the son of Montebello's uncle, Peter,<ref>Battistino (1992, 156).</ref> and a well-heeled merchant.<ref>Battistino (1992), 150, after Vella (1932), 186.</ref> He was ''Capo di Casal Tarxien'' (Head of Tarxien),<ref>Mifsud (1907), 243; Vella (1932), 187.</ref> elected by the gentry there<ref>Mifsud (1907), Deed before Notary Alexander Peter Spiteri, 243-4.</ref> to represent them in all administrative matters.<ref>''Ibid.'', Deed before Notary Gregorio Mifsud, 251.</ref> During the French presence in [[Malta]] (1798), he was chosen to be part of the committee administering one of the twelve municipalities created by [[Napoleon]], that which included Tarxien, Żejtun, [[Żabbar]] and [[Għaxaq]].<ref>Battistino (1992), 150</ref> Only three months later, however, Montebello was very much involved in the organised [[Siege of Malta (1798–1800)|resistance of the Maltese against the French]] between 1798 and 1800. As head of the local provisional government at Tarxien,<ref>Mifsud (1907), 251.</ref> he was appointed ''capo battaglione'' (battalion leader) with operational responsibilities around that locality.<ref>''Ibid.''</ref> Together with others, he contributed financially to the two-year war effort,<ref>Battistino (1992), 201.</ref> and also donated (on 24 December 1798) a considerable part of his wealth to procure wheat and other supplies from [[Sicily]] to ease the food shortage that ensued from the revolt.<ref>Testa (1980), Deed before Notary Gregorio Mifsud, 194–198</ref> When the British provisionally took over the government of the [[Maltese islands]] instead of the French Republican Commission, Giuseppe was elected by the gentry at Tarxien (18 February 1799) to be head of their locality, and thus part of the National Congress created by the representative of the British provisional government, [[Alexander Ball]].<ref>Castagna (1985), vol. II, 381.</ref> Later, Giuseppe was appointed ''Logotenente di Governo'' (Government Lieutenant) of Tarxien.<ref>''Ibid.'', vol. III, 44.</ref> Afterwards, when the British officially became lords of the land, and partitioned the [[Maltese islands]] into six districts, Giuseppe was appointed Deputy Lieutenant of the district comprising Tarxien, [[Paola, Malta|Paola]], Żejtun, Żabbar, [[Gudja]] and [[Luqa]] (28 June 1815).<ref>Battistino (1992), 156, 269.</ref> Giuseppe's house at Tarxien, built by government funds as recompense for his share in the revolt,<ref>''Ibid.'', 201.</ref> still stands unto this day, and is a tourist attraction.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.tarxienlocalcouncil.org/?module=content&id=490|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110913022037/http://www.tarxienlocalcouncil.org/?module=content&id=490|url-status=usurped|archive-date=September 13, 2011|title = Kunsill Lokali Tarxien}}</ref>

Another influential close relative, Giuseppe Pulis Montebello (1783–1855), was Montebello's nephew.<ref>He was the son of Montebello's sister, Mary (APZ, ''Reg. Bapt.'', MS 519, f. 84<sup>r</sup>). Some sources―including Farrugia Randon (1991, 116–7, 142–3), the archives of the [[University of Malta]], and the [[National Library of Malta]]―give Giuseppe's surnames in reverse form (as Montebello Pulis), which is evidently mistaken.</ref> He was from Żejtun and resided in [[Valletta]] together with his Italian wife Carlotta Bertelli.<ref>Abela (2008), 55–6; Frendo (2004), 164–5.</ref> Giuseppe lived for many years in [[Livorno]], Italy, where he married.<ref>Abela (2008), 54–5.</ref> They had at least five children.<ref>They were Amelia, Angelo, Alfredo, Gratiulla and Olderigo. ''Ibid.'', 55–7.</ref> He and his wife settled in [[Malta]] for just a decade or so, and returned to [[Livorno]] a few months before Giuseppe's death in 1855.<ref>APZ, ''Liber Solidalità dell'Agonia'', MS 191, fol. 309, and MS 124, fol. 7, cited by ''ibid.'', 56–7. Giuseppe died on 17 July.</ref> He was a well-off and self-sufficient merchant.<ref>''Ibid.''</ref> He too was elected to the National Assembly (1849–54).<ref>Farrugia Randon (1991), 143.</ref> He was very popular with voters, obtaining the largest number of popular votes.<ref>Frendo (2004), 165.</ref> Three publications of his are known. In 1824 he published ''Chtieb il Kari Yau Dahla'al ilsien Malti'' (A Book of Maltese Reading or An Introduction to the Maltese Language);<ref>Cachia (2000), 147.</ref> in 1826 ''Trattat Fuq l'Obblighi Tal-Bniedem'' (A Treatise on the Duties of Man);<ref>''Ibid.''; Debono J. (1996), 67.</ref> and in 1847 ''Rendiconto pratico del Campo Esperimentale dell'Est'' (A practical Statement on the Experimental Camp in the East).<ref>Società Economico-Agraria. Tipografia Anglo-Maltese: Malta.</ref> The first two are credited to be the first books written entirely in the [[Maltese language]].<ref>They are reviewed by Cachia (2000), 148–51 and 151–5 respectively. See also www.akkademjatalmalti.com/page.asp?p=9023 (1924; in Maltese).</ref>

===Resistance===
Together with many others, including his uncle Giuseppe, between 1798 and 1800 Montebello was part of the [[Siege of Malta (1798–1800)|resistance of the Maltese against the French]].<ref>Mifsud (1907), Document 40, 268. Following G. Fabri, Archive of the family of A.E. Caruana.</ref> He was stationed at Żejtun (at ''Tal-Borg''),<ref>Battistino (1992), 201.</ref> and gave his share within a team of resistance fighters. The team's job was to intercept any manoeuvring by or to the French troops blockaded in [[Valletta]] through the road leading to [[Cottonera]] from the east, and to organise and manage supplies around that area. Despite some skirmishes―which had even left some casualties on both sides<ref>''Ibid.'', 151–2.</ref>―Montebello's involvement does not seem to have been military, as some suggested,<ref>Abela (2008), 54.</ref> but rather of a logistical nature. In fact, together with two others (Luigi Agius, a [[doctor of canon and civil law]], and [[Vincenzo Borg]], later a [[Companion of the Order of St. Michael and St. George]]) Montebello served as ''consultore legale'' (legal adviser) under the command of Giuseppe Abela.<ref>Mifsud (1907), 268.</ref> The team's General Headquarters was situated at San Giuseppe ([[Hamrun]]), under the general command of [[Francesco Saverio Caruana]].<ref>''Ibid.'', 267.</ref> Caruana was a [[Monsignor]]<ref>Naudi (1848), 17.</ref> who had studied [[philosophy]] under [[Dun Mikiel Xerri|Michael Xerri]].<ref>''Ibid.''</ref> He was professor of [[philosophy]] and [[mathematics]] at the [[Bishop (Catholic Church)|bishop]]'s [[seminary]] at [[Mdina]],<ref>''Ibid.'', 18.</ref> and later appointed [[Bishop (Catholic Church)|Bishop of Malta]] (1831–47).<ref>{{Catholic-hierarchy|bishop|bcarua|Bishop Francesco Saverio Caruana|21 January 2015}}</ref>

===Professor of Philosophy===

Following the French [[Malta#Knights of Malta and Napoleon|capitulation]] on 5 September 1800,<ref>Frendo (2004), 10.</ref> Montebello was appointed professor of the chair of philosophy at the [[University of Malta]]. The chair had been suspended by [[Napoleon]] on 18 June 1798,<ref>Zammit (1913), Document 9; Vella (1979), 222–3.</ref> but then reinstated by the British by [[Alexander Ball]]. On 5 November 1800,<ref>Cassar Pullicino (1958), 144–5.</ref> Montebello was chosen to be professor of [[logic]] and [[metaphysics]],<ref>AAM, vol. I, 11; vol. II, 3–4; Zammit (1913), 6. For a review of AAM, see Laferla (1938).</ref> with an [[honorarium]] of 200 [[Maltese scudo|scudi]] ''per annum''.<ref>AAM, vol. I, 12; vol. II, 3–4; Cassar Pullicino (1958), 144–5.</ref> He was chosen for this office by the newly appointed [[rector (academia)|rector]], Saverio Caruana,<ref>AAM, vol. I, 8–9; vol. II, 1–2; ''Ibid.'', 144.</ref> Montebello's former 'priest-in-arms'. This was done with the approval of [[Malta]]'s provisional government (which included Montebello's cousin, Giuseppe).<ref>Mifsud (1907), 280–1.</ref>

On the day of his appointment, 5 November,<ref>AAM, vol. I, 13; vol. II, 5; ''Ibid.'', 147–8.</ref> together with the other newly appointed professors, Montebello called on the [[rector (academia)|rector]] at his residence in [[Valletta]] to thank him for their appointments. Caruana received them most kindly and, as was formerly the practice during the time of the [[Knights Hospitallers]],<ref>Zammit (1913), 6.</ref> they all proceeded to the palace of the [[Bishop (Catholic Church)|bishop]], [[Vincenzo Labini]],<ref>{{Catholic-hierarchy|bishop|blabini|Archbishop Vincenzo Labini, O.S.Io.Hieros.|21 January 2015}}</ref> in [[Valletta]] who then administered to them the oath of office. On the following day, 6 November,<ref>AAM, vol. I, 13; vol. II, 5; Mifsud (1907), 147–8.</ref> professors, students and members of the better educated classes assembled in the main hall of the [[University of Malta]] in [[Valletta]], where the [[Augustinians|Augustinian]] Vincenzo Thei (the professor of [[moral theology]]), delivered a solemn oration for the success of the new studies. The British governor, [[Alexander Ball]], was also present for the occasion. Lectures started a week later, on 13 November, after the solemn intonation of the hymn ''[[Veni Creator Spiritus]]'' in the [[University of Malta|university]] church, also at [[Valletta]]. Then each professor went to his lecture room and gave a public lecture.

Montebello's academic remit at the [[University of Malta|university]] was of two hours every week.<ref>AAM, vol. I, 10; vol. II, 3.</ref> A welcome development occurred on 13 March 1802, when the British governor, [[Alexander Ball]], re-established the practice of conferring degrees, thus giving more weight to the academic institution. In the following month the first ceremony of the conferrement of degrees under British rule was held.<ref>Agius (1968), 11.</ref> This must have brought on, a few months later, on 5 May 1802, the increase in salary of the [[University of Malta|university]] professors, including Montebello's, from two to three hundred [[Maltese scudo|scudi]] ''per annum'' by the British Civil Commissioner, Charles Cameron.<ref>AAM, vol. I, 20-1; vol. II, 12-3.</ref> Following these developments, no other events of note seem to have occurred at the [[University of Malta|university]] up till 1813,<ref>Agius (1968), 11.</ref> well after Montebello's time there.

===Parish Priest===
In 1804, Montebello relinquished the chair of philosophy when he was appointed by [[Bishop (Catholic Church)|Bishop]] Vincenzo Labini<ref>{{Catholic-hierarchy|bishop|blabini|Archbishop Vincenzo Labini, O.S.Io.Hieros.|21 January 2015}}</ref> as parish priest of ''Civitatis Cospiquæ'' ([[Bormla]]).<ref>AAM, vol. I, 28; vol. II, 20; Tabone (2001), 67.</ref> On 3 October of that year, he was succeeded at the [[University of Malta|university]] by the professor of [[humanistic]] [[literature]] and secretary of the [[University of Malta|university]], Peter Mallia, a [[doctor of canon and civil law]].<ref>AAM, ''Ibid.''</ref>

Montebello became vicar (or ''Parochus prælectus'')<ref>APB, ''Reg. Bapt.'', vol. 2, fol. 274.</ref> of [[Bormla]] on 23 June 1804,<ref>APB, ''Reg. Matrim.'', vol. 8, fol. 135<sup>r</sup> "infra".</ref> and immediately took up residence there<ref>APB, ''Reg. Bapt.'', vol. 2, fol. 274.</ref> together with his sister Vincenza. He took official possession of the parish (as ''Parochus et Rector'')<ref>''Ibid.'', fol. 277.</ref> on the following 26 July.<ref>APB, ''Reg. Matrim.'', vol. 8, fol. 135<sup>r</sup> "infra"; Ferres (1866, 301) mistakenly gives the possession day to be the 27th.</ref> He was the sixteenth parish priest of [[Bormla]]<ref>Tabone (2001), 67.</ref> since the [[parish]]'s inception on 15 September 1586.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.cospicuaparish.org.mt/thecity.asp.|title=Is-sit uffiċċjali tal-Kolleġġjata Perinsinji ta' Marija Immakulata – Belt l-Immakulata}}</ref> However, as it happened, he was also its last parish priest, since in 1822, during the tenure of Montebello's successor as parish priest, Giuseppe Bezzina, the [[parish]] became a [[Collegiate church|Collegiate]] by [[Decree#Catholic Church|decree]] of [[Pope Pius VII]].<ref>Tabone (2001), 13.</ref>

Apart from the usual pastoral duties as parish priest, at [[Bormla]], Montebello founded, in May 1805, the [[Confraternity]] of [[St. Agatha]]<ref>Ferres (1866), 299; Camilleri (2001).</ref> and a few months later, on 15 September 1805, the [[Confraternity]] of [[Saint Michael (Roman Catholic)|St. Michael]].<ref>Ferres (1866), 299.</ref>

===Death===
Montebello remained parish priest for five years.<ref>Tabone (2001), 72.</ref> He died suddenly and prematurely at his residence in [[Bormla]]<ref>APPV, ''Reg. Defun.'', vol. 14, fol. 452.</ref> on 18 April 1809,<ref>APB, ''Reg. Defun.'', vol. 2, fol. 75; ACB, ''Registrum Musicæ'' [''Reg. Mus.''], vol. 24, no. 47; Ferres (1866), 301.</ref> aged 46,<ref>ACB, ''Reg. Mus.'', vol. 24, no. 47.</ref> Though the last baptism he administered was just two days before his death, on the April 16,<ref>APB, ''Reg. Bapt.'', vol. 2, fol. 503.</ref> he was apparently too ill to officiate at a marriage celebrated on April 11.<ref>APB, ''Reg. Matrim.'', vol. 8, f. 298.</ref> Oddly enough, his funeral was not held at [[Bormla]], as would have been normal practice, but at the parish church of his birthplace, Żejtun, with the participation of the [[Clergy#Catholicism|clergy]] serving at [[Bormla]].<ref>ACB, ''Reg. Mus.'', vol. 24, no. 47.</ref> Stranger still, for some reason yet unknown he was not buried at Żejtun but was transported again, this time to [[Valletta]], and buried in the crypt of the [[Collegiate church]] of [[Collegiate Parish Church of St Paul's Shipwreck|St. Paul's Shipwreck]],<ref>''Ibid.''; APB, ''Reg. Defun.'', vol. 2, fol. 75.</ref> in the part reserved for priests.<ref>APPV, ''Reg. Defun.'', vol. 14, fol. 452 (''in sepulcro Sacerdotorum'').</ref> In gratitude towards the [[Clergy#Catholicism|clergy]] of [[Bormla]], a few days after the funeral, on the 23 April, his sister, Vincenza Montebello, donated 50 [[Maltese scudo|scudi]] to the [[Bormla]] collagate ''per i poveri di Cospicua'' (for the poor of [[Bormla]]).<ref>ACB, ''Reg. Mus.'', vol. 24, no. 47.</ref> Several masses were sung by the [[Bormla]] [[Clergy#Catholicism|clergy]] for his repose on the anniversary of his death in the succeeding five years (until 1814).<ref>''Ibid.''</ref> More masses were sung for his repose by the clergy at Żejtun almost fifty years later, in 1855, and in succeeding years, by bequest of Giuseppe Pulis Montebello.<ref>APZ, MS 175, fols. 167–181 (following the Deed before Notary Salvatore Tanti), and MS 231, cited by Abela (2008), 56.</ref>

==Works==
There is as yet no indication that Montebello ever published any works, philosophical or otherwise. In all probability he did not.

His class notes on [[logic]] and [[metaphysics]], subjects which he taught for four years at the [[University of Malta]], do not seem to have survived, not even in indirect form (by his students). At least, nothing is yet known about their whereabouts. Having said this, however, it might not be irrelevant to point out that the hundreds of manuscripts held at the archive of the [[Collegiate church|Collegiate]] of [[Bormla]]―one likely place where Montebello's writings might be held―are still not catalogued. This, as yet, makes it impossible to know for sure whether anything of his philosophical notes survived. To date, it is not known whether Montebello drew up any [[last will]], as was usually done.<ref>Given the archival circumstances in [[Malta]], manual research in this regard will have to cover the period from 1778/80 (when Montebello reached the [[Age of majority|legal age]] of 16/18 to draw up a [[Will (law)|will]]) or when his last parent (his mother) died, up till 1809 (25/27 years and more), an endeavour which is at present unfeasible.</ref>
